Without adequate treatment, this patient will be at increased risk for developing which of the following?

                    ### Question
                    A 12-year-old boy presents to the pediatrician for a routine checkup. He and his family immigrated from Pakistan to the United States when he was 9 years of age. Per his mother, he had measles when he was 4 years of age and a high fever following a sore throat at the age 7. He received all appropriate vaccinations when he arrived in the United States. He takes no medications. He does well academically and plays soccer in a recreational league. He was born at 38 weeks gestation. His temperature is 98.4°F (36.9°C), blood pressure is 115/65 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 18/min. On exam, he is a healthy boy in no apparent distress. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally with good aeration. Fixed splitting of the second heart sound is noted on auscultation. Without adequate treatment, this patient will be at increased risk for developing which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Acute endocarditis
opb. Extra-cardiac left-to-right shunting
opc. Mitral regurgitation
opd. Mitral stenosis
ope. Reversal of left-to-right shunting

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The presence of fixed splitting of the second heart sound in this 12-year-old boy suggests a possible atrial septal defect (ASD), which is a common cause of left-to-right shunting. This condition leads to increased blood flow to the right heart, resulting in right heart volume overload and potential complications such as pulmonary hypertension. If left untreated, the increased pulmonary blood flow can lead to pulmonary vascular disease and eventually result in reversal of the left-to-right shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome). While acute endocarditis can occur in the context of heart failure, it is not a direct consequence of ASD. Mitral regurgitation may develop due to left heart overload, but it is not the primary concern in this scenario. Therefore, the most relevant risk associated with untreated ASD is the potential for reversal of left-to-right shunting, making option (ope) the most appropriate choice.
